signal, and far more targeted validations (ex. using CLAP), specifically of sites not recapitulated
by other datasets.
Our response:
We are grateful for the constructive feedback from reviewer #1. The reviewer has noted a 4%
and 8% overlap between our data and previously reported sites for HeLa and 293T mRNA,
respectively. The lower percentage of overlap is attributed to a greater number of sites identified
by our method due to its higher sensitivity, which we view as an advantageous feature.
In this revised version of manuscript, we performed a comparative analysis with the three most
recently published bisulfite-based methods (BID-seq, RBS-seq, and PRAISE). Our method
demonstrated substantial coverage, and successfully identified 42%, 49%, and 60% of the
reported sites, respectively (Figure S10a). Overall, our data encompassed 1,904 of the 4,333
previously reported sites for 293T mRNA (combined data from BID-seq, PRAISE and CeU-seq)
(Figure S10a). Our dataset not only validated these modification sites but also facilitated the
precise localization of Ψ modifications within multiple Us, a challenging task for the current
bisulfite-based approaches.
To address discrepancies with previous methods, we further looked at signals of PRAISE-unique
sites in our dataset. Our data uncovered 1,237 of the 2,070 sites reported by PRAISE (Figure S10
a-b). Among the 833 PRAISE-unique sites, 526 exhibited prominent stop signatures in at least
one replicate of our data, with 113 showing signals in two replicates. However, these sites were
excluded from our final list due to being present in only one replicate or having low read
coverage (Figure S10e). Only 288 sites (13.9%) lacked any signal in our dataset, and these sites
were found to have lower deletion ratios and read coverage than the rest Ψ sites in the PRAISE-
seq dataset (Figure S10f), suggesting that they are intrinsically more difficult to identify and may
have lower confidence. Our examination also identified 11 sites determined by PRAISE that
were covered by multi-mapped reads, potentially leading to repeated counts, and 8 sites flagged
as false positives due to identical stop signatures in both the pull-down and input in our data.
Similarly, for the 302 BID-unique sites, we identified 65 additional sites showing prominent stop
signals in at least one replicate of our dataset, with those lacking signals in our dataset mainly
situated in unfavorable sequence contexts and displaying low deletion levels in BID-seq dataset.
Furthermore, our data covered 70% of TruB1 sites reported by PRAISE (Figure S10h) and all
mitochondria mRNA sites reported by PRAISE and BID-seq (Supplementary table 3-4).
Notably, by comparing the U sites and non-U sites identified by our method, we found that
increasing cutoff for stop ratio could increase the degree of confidence for the reported sites
(Figure 4 g-h). Additionally, by performing a third replicate for each cell line, we found that the
degree of confidence increases with the number of replicates (Figure 4i). This suggests a means
to better characterize the authenticity of each candidate site. Based on these observations, we
more stringently defined the degree of confidence for each candidate Ψ site based on the stop
ratio and the number of replicates the site can be repetitively identified in. Among the 10106
sites identified from HeLa cells, 4260 are defined as “highest-confidence” sites as they fulfil
both criteria of being identified in all three biological replicates and having stop ratios higher
than 0.3, 3801 sites are defined as “higher-confidence” sites for fulfilling one of the criteria, and
2044 are defined as “lower-confidence sites” for fulfilling none of the criteria (Figure 4j and
Lines 329-336).
The assignment of confidence, coupled with the enhanced accuracy in estimating the
modification levels as addressed in the response to question #2 from reviewer #1, provides
valuable insights for characterizing each individual candidate site.
Upon inspecting raw signals in BID-seq for 6,333 ELAP-seq-only higher or highest-confidence
sites, we found that 3,012 sites showed deletion ratio of higher than 0.05 in at least one replicate
of BID-seq, thus these sites demonstrate modification signals in BID-seq as well (Figure S10j).
Among the rest sites, 2,139 sites have deletion ratio of between 0.0 and 0.05 in BID-seq with
82% of them having average deletion ratios among three replicates of between 0.02 to 0.05,
which is below the deletion ratio cutoff used by the method (Figure S10j). There are 1,182 sites
having deletion ratio of 0 in BID-seq data, and these sites exhibited substantially lower read
coverage than sites detected by BID-seq, suggesting that these sites were missed by BID-seq due
to low gene expression (Figure S10k). This further supports the authenticity of sites identified by
ELAP-seq and underscores the high sensitivity of our approach in validating weak signals in
BID-seq.
In addition to more thorough data analysis, we also performed CLAP and CMC-RT-qPCR
validation for more sites. In addition to the ten sites presented in the previous version, we
evaluated 1 more site using CLAP (Figure S9c) and 7 more sites using CMC-RT-qPCR (Figure
S7f). Overall, 18 sites were successfully validated, including 10 sites not previously identified by
any method.
We have incorporated the above results in the revised manuscript (Lines 398-433), as well as
detailed discussions for the origins of false positives and false negatives to address concerns
users might have when approaching our dataset or using our method (Lines 573-607).
In response to reviewer’s suggestions, we employed siRNA knockdown (KD) of TruB1 and
DKC1 and strived to assess the dependence of our reported sites on PUS to further prove their
authenticity. Unfortunately, we have encountered unforeseen technical issues which have
delayed our data acquisition. We believe that the significant improvements we have made would
have already sufficiently addressed the concerns raised by the reviewers. Therefore, we are
submitting this revised manuscript without the inclusion of data from the PUS KD studies.
However, we are still actively acquiring data from the PUS KD experiments and will be willing
to provide the data if the reviewers see them remain necessary and critical.
We believe that this revised manuscript has been substantially improved by: 1) a more rigorous
characterization of the confidence level for each candidate site; 2) a comprehensive comparison
of our dataset with PRAISE and BID-seq to address the discrepancies; 3) improved accuracy in
quantifying the modification levels; 4) thorough evaluation of the reproducibility of our method;
5) site-specific validation of more sites not captured by other methods; 6) detailed discussions of
the origins of false negatives and false positives; as well as 7) streamlined pipeline with a single
command for user-friendly analysis. We believe these revisions have greatly increased the
usability of our dataset and the reliability of our method.
In summary, our revision includes additional experiments, meticulous data analysis, and detailed
discussions, reinforcing the validity of the identified sites. Moreover, our method excels in
detecting sites overlooked by other methodologies albeit may be less effective in identifying sites
in less favorable sequence contexts, especially those with low modification levels. We posit that
our method represents a potent innovation and serves as a crucial complement to the existing
toolbox for RNA modification detection and investigation.
2. The authors claim that 1/3 of sites have over a 50% modification rate, much higher than the
average mRNA modification rates estimated from other methods such as BID-Seq, and
inconsistent with their claim that the massive number of new sites are from enrichment of lowly-
modified positions. The authors must more rigorously demonstrate that their estimation of
modification occupancy is accurate, by correlating their estimates with estimates from
mutational-profiling methods such as BID-Seq, and by demonstrating correlation with many
more than 2 sites estimated by CLAP. Also, the CLAP vs ELAP-Seq comparison is difficult to
see in figure 4h and should have its own figure panel (with the additional comparisons).
Our response:
Thank the reviewer for this constructive critique. In response to the reviewer's critique, we
conducted a correlation analysis comparing the quantification results obtained from ELAP-seq
with those from CLAP and PRAISE (Lines 379-397). We performed CLAP and obtained
absolute quantification for one mRNA modification site (Figure S9c). In addition, there are 9
other mRNA modification sites quantified by CALP previously. All these 10 mRNA sites are in
non-ΨU sequence context. Notably, we observed a strong correlation between ELAP-seq and
CLAP quantifications for these sites (r = 0.83) (Figure 4m). Additionally, we correlated
quantification by our method to that by PRAISE due to a high number of overlapping sies. While
the correlations for sites within non-ΨU contexts were moderate (r = 0.46-0.56), the correlation
was high for sites within ΨU contexts (r = 0.72) (Figure S9d). These results, combined with the
observation that highly modified rRNA sites are distributed at the upper end of the quantification
spectrum, underscore the general accuracy of quantification by ELAP-seq.
Our method relies on adjusted enrichment levels to estimate the relative modification levels,
rather than determining exact modification ratios, a limitation of pull-down based strategies.
Nevertheless, by utilizing the absolute quantification provided by CLAP (for non-ΨU context
sites) and PRAISE (for ΨU context sites) as benchmarks, we were able to estimate the
approximate modification levels more confidently in this revised manuscript. This analysis
revealed that approximately 20-25% of sites exhibit moderate modification levels (between 30%-
60%) or high modification levels (exceeding 60%), while over 70% of sites are characterized as
lowly modified (below 30%) (Figure S9e). These results align more closely with conclusions
drawn from other studies (PMID: 36997645 and 36302989). Such semi-quantitative estimations
of modification levels, coupled with the capacity to probe modification level changes across
conditions, would render our method applicable to a wide range of studies.
With the improved quantification accuracy, we re-examined enriched GO terms for genes
containing moderately and highly modified Ψ, and found a notable enrichment of categories
related to mitochondrial electron transport and ATP synthesis (Figure 5e) (Lines 459-470). This
finding aligns with the report that PUS1 is associated with mitochondrial myopathy and calls for
future investigation into the roles of Ψ in mitochondrial function and associated diseases.
3. The language explaining the rational for cutoffs and filtering is vague. Please provide specific
details with statistical justification for the following: “We optimized cutoffs for stop ratio and
reads coverage and allow for gradients of coverage for different ranges of stop ratios” [275-276]
“We required higher reads coverage for lower levels of stop ratios to decrease false positives”
[685-686] “We allowed slightly lower reads coverage for sites in the out-group” [688-689]
“…we screened cutoffs for stop ratios and coverage to find a balance between the number of
sites identified and percentage of U” [689-691]
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewers' feedback regarding the clarity of cutoffs and filtering rationale. The
cutoffs were determined empirically. Initially, we set a stop ratio of 0.1, guided by our visual
examination of IGV, which indicated that some clustered sites tended to exhibit low stop ratios.
Additionally, we allowed a read coverage of 5, a practice used in several other studies (PMID:
31548705 and 26075521). However, upon using the percentage of U as an indicator, we found
these cutoffs to be suboptimal (U% = 81%). Consequently, we further refined them with more
stringent cutoffs. The rationale behind this optimization was requiring higher read coverage for
sites with lower stop ratios. In addition, in-group sites situated inside of the enrichment peaks
typically had higher read coverage, thus necessitating overall higher coverage thresholds for
these sites. As the number of sites detected decreases with increasing U%, we settled on cutoffs
which gave U% of 87.9%. The script used has been provided in GitHub and the cutoffs can be
further user-defined for desired confidence. For example, users may raise the cutoffs for stop
ratio to filter for sites with higher confidence.
We have now provided the specific details in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 875-
880):“…The optimized process was as follows: 1) we required higher reads coverage for lower
levels of stop ratios to decrease rate of false positives: In-group: at least 6-read coverage for sites
with stop ratios > 0.8, at least 8-read coverage for sites with stop ratios ranging between 0.2 and
0.8 , and stopped reads of at least 11 for sites with stop ratios ranging between 0.1 and 0.2; Out-
group: at least 5-read coverage for sites with stop ratios > 0.8, at least 7-read coverage for sites
with stop ratios ranging between 0.2 and 0.8 , and stopped reads of at least 2 for sites with stop
ratios ranging between 0.1 and 0.2; …”
4. For the IFN dataset it is mentioned that “the interferon stimulated samples (IFN+) resulted in
~40% less reads compared to untreated samples (IFN-), thus we allowed lower reads coverage
cutoff for the IFN+ samples.”[715-719] How does this not increase the false positive rate for the
INF+ samples – if the read cutoffs were set to minimize false positive rate? Intuitively this cutoff
should not be determined by read depth. This comparison would be more accurate with the INF-
samples randomly sub-sampled down to the same depth as INF+, using identical read cutoffs.
Our response:
This is a great point. In the previous version of the manuscript, we implemented a stricter cutoff
for IFN- samples and a looser cutoff for IFN+ samples, based on the established thresholds used
for HeLa and HEK cell lines. As noted by the reviewer, this adjustment could lead to an
increased rate of false negatives and false positives for each sample group, respectively. In this
revised manuscript, we reverted to the original cutoffs, resulting in the identification of 9117 and
3737 candidate sites from IFN- and IFN+ samples, respectively (Figure 6c and Lines 498-501).
To ensure more accurate comparisons, we conducted a reanalysis of the data by employing an
equal number of sub-sampled reads for both IFN- and IFN+ samples. Utilizing the same pipeline
with consistent read cutoffs, we reanalyzed data subsampled from reads of libraries constructed
with SuperScript III, or combined libraries built with SuperScript III and SuperScript IV. In both
scenarios, we observed a 40~50% reduction in identified sites from the IFN+ samples compared
to the IFN- samples (Figure S12b and lines 501-503). This finding supports a consistent trend of
downregulation of Ψ following interferon treatment, which aligns with observations made using
LC-MS/MS.
Minor critiques:
1. “a significant proportion of Ψ sites in mRNA appear in the 5’-ΨU-3’ context…” [203-204]
what proportion exactly?
Our response: Based on the paper of Li et al., ~30% of Ψ sites appear in the 5’ ΨU 3’ context.
We have changed our main text to provide a more precise description (Lines 209-210).
2. “30 – 60% of Ψ in cellular mRNA can be labeled by this enzyme” [205-206] Do you expect
30-60% of Ψ positions are being labeled – or each site is being labeled at a 30-60% rate?
Our response:
We apologize for the confusion caused by this sentence. The ratio 30-60% is m1Ψ/Ψ percentage
determined through LC-MS/MS analysis on digested RNAs. Due to the sequence preference of
the enzyme, the efficiency of enzymatic labeling should be higher for Ψ sites in the 5’-ΨU-3’
context compared to sites in other sequence contexts. Ψ sites in the 5’-ΨU-3’ constitutes around
30% of all Ψ sites in mRNA while Ψ sites in other sequence contexts constitutes about 70%.
Therefore, more than 30% of Ψ sites would undergo labeling, with the degree of labeling at
individual positions contingent upon the specific sequence context, which together gave an
overall labeling efficiency of 30-60% across all Ψ sites.
We have modified our main text to clarify this (Line 139): “The overall 33-60% m1Ψ/Ψ ratio
suggests that a considerable proportion of Ψ modification sites were successfully labeled.”
3. Why is there a stop in untreated RNA at the expected psi position in figure 2e?
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewer's observation, and upon reflection, we acknowledge that our
manuscript lacked clarity in describing the experiment's design.
In our assay, we used a synthetic 33-mer RNA as the template, which harbors a Ψ modification
in the middle. A fluorescently labeled RT primer was designed to target the position immediately
downstream of the modification site. The RT primer and template were mixed at a 1:10 ratio to
drive most primers to hybridize with the template. In the absence of any treatment, the RT primer
reads through the modification site, producing the full-length RT product (upper FL band).
Conversely, when encountering the propargyl-Ψ adduct (with or without subsequent
biotinylation at a low dNTP concentration), the elongation of the RT primer is impeded, resulting
in a significant amount of un-extended RT primer (lower Primer band in Figure 2e).
The anticipated stop signatures in treated RNA align precisely with the expected Ψ position. The
limited presence of un-extended RT primer bands in untreated RNAs is likely attributed to a low
level of unhybridized RT primer (Figure 2e, lane 2 and lane 6). Notably, the un-extended RT
primer bands in treated RNAs exhibited considerably stronger signals compared to those in
untreated RNAs (Figure 2e, lane 3-5 compared to lane 2, and lanes 7-9 compared to lane 6). This
disparity indicates that the introduction of bulkier groups during Ψ labeling significantly
increased the arrest rate of reverse transcription at the modification site, aligning with our
expectations.
To make the experimental design clearer, we have incorporated additional details in the legend
of Figure 2 and in the Materials and Method section (Lines 714-724).
4. How do the NNpsiNN pools perform in the standard library prep? E.g. are there any RT-stop
or ligation biases due to sequence context?
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewer's insightful question. In assessing the sequence preference of
enzymatic labeling with the NNpsiNN pools, we employed a protocol designed to avoid
generating RT stops so that we could comprehensively evaluate the sequence context spectrum
on both sides of the modification site. Specifically, following on-bead pull-down, we eluted
RNAs from the beads by heat-denaturing the streptavidin-biotin interaction. Subsequently, we
employed Superscript IV with 0.5 mM final dNTP to facilitate full readthrough at the
modification site. Additional details about this methodology have been incorporated into the
Materials and Methods section for clarification (Lines 816-817).
Our ELAP-seq results consistently identified uracil as the primary nucleobase, aligning with the
in vitro characterization of Mj1640's specificity towards Ψ. This evidence supports the
conclusion that ELAP-seq specifically detects Ψ sites in RNA. We want to emphasize that, in our
library preparation workflow, we do not perceive sequence context-dependent biases in RT-stop
or ligation. While previous studies have reported sequence biases for 3’ RNA adapter ligation
using T4 RNA ligase 2 truncated KQ, we mitigated this bias by employing RNA adapters with
multiple Ns on the 5’ end, as recommended (Nucleic Acids Research, 2011, Nov; 39(21):e141).
Our analysis of input libraries using the same pipeline revealed no enrichment for uracil,
demonstrating that ligation and reverse transcription were not influenced by sequence context.
5. It is not described how the wobble pair analysis was performed, please add more detail in the
methods or main text.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have now provided a more detailed description
of the analysis in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 934-946). We have also deposited the
data analysis pipelines and the in-house python transcripts to GitHub.
“RNA sequences of 100 nt surrounding all Ψ sites located in different mRNA subregions (5’
UTR, 3’ UTR and CDS) with 50 nt upstream and 50 nt downstream were used for RNA
secondary structure prediction. The program viennaRNA was used with the command of
‘RNAfold -p < input.fa > output.res’. The resulting file was cleaned up in notepad++ to keep the
information of the topmost prediction for each site. Then, we used an in-house python script
match.py to extract the information of the base pairing status of the modification site and the
location of its matched base if it is base paired. We then determined the identity of the matched
base for each base-paired modification site using the ‘MID’ function in excel. Next, we
calculated the frequency of the modification site residing in a mismatched/UG wobble status
versus in UA matched status. Control U sites were chosen at both the -20 position and +20
position of Ψ sites and analysis were performed the same way as for Ψ sites. mfold were used to
draw the secondary structures of 100 nt surrounding the chosen Ψ sites.”
6. Enrichment of Ψ at splice junctions is only informative with a comparison against the
background distribution of U. Plot both distributions from your dataset and demonstrate that the
difference in Ψ distribution is significant.
Our response:
We express gratitude to the reviewer for providing valuable insights into the analysis. In
response to the suggestion, we randomly selected 10,000 U sites from the transcriptome and
conducted a parallel analysis. To our disappointment, these randomly chosen sites were also
found to be situated within 100 nt of the nearest splice sites. To delve deeper into this
observation, we computed the average distance to splice sites within 800 nt, 400 nt, 200 nt, and
100 nt windows, and still, no substantial differences were observed between the Ψ group and the
control U groups across any of these window sizes. We regret the oversight that led to an
incorrect conclusion in the previous version of the manuscript. To rectify this, we have removed
the erroneous figure and texts that depicted the correlation of Ψ with splicing.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
During revision, the authors have incorporated a substantial number of bioinformatics analyses. These analyses encompass overlap studies with the PRAISE, BID-seq, and CeU-seq methodologies. Additionally, the authors have performed DKC1 knockdown experiments to identified PUS-dependent sites.The potential false positives and false negatives associated with the technology have been thoroughly discussed in the discussion section. However, two minor concerns remain to be addressed:
1. The authors should provide data from NNUNN spike-in experiments to further validate the specificity of the technology.
2. In Figure S8b, despite the authors having performed three replicates, the reproducibility of the modification sites is only approximately 20%. A detailed explanation and clarification of this discrepancy are required.
(Remarks on code availability)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, Wang et al. present a new transcriptome-wide pseudouridine (Ψ) site profiling method (ELAP-seq) using the Mj1640 enzyme to modify Ψ sites with a propargyl group and click-chemistry for biotin labeling. The authors achieved enrichment of Ψ by streptavidin pulldown and single nucleotide resolution by harnessing the RT-stop signature. For the most part, the authors have addressed concerns voiced by Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 3. The most appealing finding in this current manuscript is the detection of many more Ψ sites compared to previous methods, with some sites further validated by orthogonal methods. However, the potential strength of this enzyme-based method appears to be underdeveloped, and the inconsistency of cutoffs and filtering makes it difficult to follow. These concerns, combined with the relative simplicity, quantitativeness, and cost-effectiveness without need for commercially unavailable enzyme of other methods (particularly bisulfite-Ψ adduct methods PRAISE for transcriptome-wide Ψ profiling and BID-Seq for targeted Ψ profiling) severely limit the utility of ELAP-seq to the Ψ research community.
As such, the current version of this manuscript is not well suited for publication in this journal, in our opinion. The manuscript would be more useful as either a resource of novel Ψ sites (which would require a lot more validation, particularly for lower confidence sites) or a revelation of novel biology that existing methods cannot capture.
Major comments:
1. The authors claim that ELAP-seq could be used in live cells for Ψ profiling, but in the ELAP-Seq protocol they denature fragmented isolated RNA prior to enzymatic labeling. This is a contradiction, because RNA secondary structure is influenced by conditions unique to cells not present in denatured fragmented isolated RNA, including long-range RNA-RNA interactions and RNA-binding proteins. For this reason, it is not obvious to the reader that in situ ELAP-Seq would work. Certainly in vivo ELAP-Seq, as hinted at in Supplementary Fig. S3, would not work.
2. In the Introduction, the authors emphasize that many other methods for profiling Ψ sites require a high level of RNA input and/or deep sequencing. Although the authors showed the detection sensitivity of this assay on synthesized oligos in Figure 2b, the detection limit of this assay on real mRNA samples from cells is unclear (based on the Methods section, ELAP-seq appears to be carried out with 200-1000ng of RNA, but it is unclear if it is total RNA or isolated mRNA). In this aspect, it remains uncertain whether ELAP-seq can be used for rare cell populations that other methods could hardly approach.
3. In lines 234-236 the authors decided to use data generated with Superscript III for detecting Ψ sites, while in lines 287-289 the authors decided to combine Superscript III and Superscript IV data to yield better signal. The inconsistency of data analysis makes it difficult to follow. It might be better to fix a filtering and cutoff strategy with rRNA benchmarking and then stick to the same filtering so that the level of false positives can be more easily estimated.
4. In lines 278-280 and a few cases later in the manuscript, as well as in Fig. 4c-e, the authors detected Ψ sites at U, G, A, C with different proportions, while when describing their filter strategy (lines 246-247) they only include sites for which “the stop event occurs at uridine (U).” It is unclear why these G, A, C sites were still included with their pipeline, unless the authors really mean ΨU, ΨG, ΨA, and ΨC.
5. In the paragraphs to study Ψ sites in response to IFN treatment, the phenotype was not well explained. By LS-MS/MS, there seemed to be a 20-25% reduction of global Ψ, while by ELAP-seq there seemed to be 41-52% fewer sites. The authors should explain this discrepancy. Additionally, since the protein level of PUS enzymes did not change, it is unclear how robust this assay was. The authors should either demonstrate Ψ change with a different method or identify other enzymes/regulators to explain the phenotype.
6. Pull-down of both enzymatic and control reactions in ELAP-seq means that the methodology will likely be even less quantitative than other semi-quantitative methods for lower RNA inputs. It is hard to imagine that spike-ins mentioned in lines 564-565 would alleviate this concern.
Minor comments:
1. In the rebuttal, the authors write that, “Performed knockdown experiment for one of the pseudouridine writers, DKC1, which led to the identification of 1014 sites confidently downregulated due to DKC1 depletion, including 882 sites newly identified by ELAP-seq (Figure 4h and the new supplementary Figure S10).” The authors should analyze how much of this change is due to transcript expression changes leading to lower confidence in calling Ψ sites vs. bona fide Ψ downregulation.
2. In line 114, the authors write, “data not shown.” They should show the data or remove/restate the sentence.
3. In line 232-234, the authors do not show Superscript IV data.
4. The authors should state the precise statistical test used to generate the p-value stated in line 241.
5. In line 466, Fig. 5f should be Fig. 5e.
6. In the Discussion in lines 604-605, the authors speculate that Mj1640 could be used to selectively introduce m1Ψ to mRNA vaccines. It is hard to imagine that such a strategy would be productive, given that such a change would inherently increase immunogenicity and reduce protein translational efficiency.
(Remarks on code availability)

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful comments that helped us substantially
improve this manuscript and strengthen the practical value of ELAP-seq. In this revision,
we have:
 Included additional biochemical characterization data (Figure S4) and control
spike-in data (Figure S5), further validating the sensitivity and specificity of the
technology.
 Improved reproducibility assessment with additional data analysis, addressing the
discrepancies across replicates.
 Refined and benchmarked the data processing pipeline and applied it uniformly
across all datasets, making the analysis consistent and the interpretation of false
positive rate more reliable.
 Provided further clarification of input requirements, quantification capabilities,
and enzyme accessibility considerations for ELAP-seq.
 Refined the discussion of potential applications to avoid overstating in-cell
applicability and to include additional applications suggested by new data.
 Responded to other comments raised by the reviewers, including clarifying
specific points of the experimental design and data analysis workflow.
Below we address each comment point-by-point.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
During revision, the authors have incorporated a substantial number of bioinformatics
analyses. These analyses encompass overlap studies with the PRAISE, BID-seq, and
CeU-seq methodologies. Additionally, the authors have performed DKC1 knockdown
experiments to identify PUS-dependent sites.The potential false positives and false
negatives associated with the technology have been thoroughly discussed in the
discussion section. However, two minor concerns remain to be addressed:
1. The authors should provide data from NNUNN spike-in experiments to further validate
the specificity of the technology.
Our response: We have conducted ELAP-seq on the NNUNN spike-in, added a new
figure (Figure S5) to report the result and incorporated this result in the main text.
Importantly, no specific sequence was enriched for the NNUNN spike-in, in clear
contrast to the enrichment pattern observed for NNΨNN spike-in. Moreover, compared
with the NNΨNN libraries, both the NNUNN and its click control (mock click chemistry)
libraries were built with overamplification. Altogether, these results suggest that there is
no specific labeling or enrichment of the NNUNN spike-in oligos.
The high specificity of the enzymatic labeling assay was also demonstrated by the new
data added in Figure S4 comparing labeling on modified vs unmodified RNAs (in the
NNΨ/UNN context) in dot blot assays.
2. In Figure S8b, despite the authors having performed three replicates, the
reproducibility of the modification sites is only approximately 20%. A detailed
explanation and clarification of this discrepancy are required.
Our response: Thanks to the reviewers for this insightful question. We noticed that some
sites with low read coverage may lack any coverage in other replicates simply due to
technical variation, leading to low overlap. To remove the effect of technical variation at
low-coverage sites and better evaluate reproducibility in identifying modification-specific
signals, we focused on sites covered by at least five reads in at least one other replicate
(within our filtering criterion of ≥5 stopped reads) and then applied our standard filter
criteria for calling RT stop sites. This updated analysis yielded markedly improved
reproducibility: approximately 64% of stop sites in each replicate were detected in at
least one other replicate, and 32–39% of sites were shared across all three replicates
(Figure S10c).
To further address the remaining discrepancies, we examined RT stop sites identified in
only one replicate. Because RT stop sites are defined mainly based on the number of
stopped reads and the stop ratio, we compared the number of stopped reads between sites
unique to a single replicate and those detected in multiple replicates. For example, sites
identified only in replicate 1 (Rep1-only sites) exhibited substantially fewer stopped
reads than sites also detected in other replicates, and most fell below the detection
threshold in the other replicates (Figure S10d). This indicates that the discrepancies
mainly arise from sites with near-threshold stopped reads counts. In this study, we define
candidate modification sites as those detected in at least two independent replicates,
which effectively enriches for sites with robust signals.
These updated results are now shown in Figure S10b-d. We have added this explanation
to the main text (page 16, lines 317-322). The associated code was also updated in Github
(code availability section).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Wang et al. present a new transcriptome-wide pseudouridine (Ψ) site
profiling method (ELAP-seq) using the Mj1640 enzyme to modify Ψ sites with a
propargyl group and click-chemistry for biotin labeling. The authors achieved
enrichment of Ψ by streptavidin pulldown and single nucleotide resolution by harnessing
the RT-stop signature. For the most part, the authors have addressed concerns voiced by
Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 3. The most appealing finding in this current manuscript is the
detection of many more Ψ sites compared to previous methods, with some sites further
validated by orthogonal methods. However, the potential strength of this enzyme-based
method appears to be underdeveloped, and the inconsistency of cutoffs and filtering
makes it difficult to follow. These concerns, combined with the relative simplicity,
quantitativeness, and cost-effectiveness without need for commercially unavailable
enzyme of other methods (particularly bisulfite-Ψ adduct methods PRAISE for
transcriptome-wide Ψ profiling and BID-Seq for targeted Ψ profiling) severely limit the
utility of ELAP-seq to the Ψ research community. As such, the current version of this
manuscript is not well suited for publication in this journal, in our opinion. The
manuscript would be more useful as either a resource of novel Ψ sites (which would
require a lot more validation, particularly for lower confidence sites) or a revelation of
novel biology that existing methods cannot capture.
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We would like to address the
reviewers’ concerns as below:
Utility of ELAP-seq: We have successfully applied the method to multiple cell lines and
conditions, reproducing many previously reported Ψ sites and uncovering new ones,
many of which have been directly or indirectly validated. These newly detected sites will
provide a valuable resource and can guide future targeted investigations using low-
throughput assays (e.g., CMC-based primer extension assays). Notably, 10% of ELAP-
seq identified sites are of low confidence, thus the majority of sites are reliable.
While enrichment-based approaches are semi-quantitative, they have been highly
informative for RNA modification studies, such as the MeRIP-seq method for profiling
N6-methyladenosine. Based on the existing data and new data presented in Figure S4 and
S5, ELAP-seq shows improved specificity and sensitivity and will outperform previous
chemical- or antibody-based enrichment strategies.
Mj1640 is highly stable and can be readily prepared in most molecular biology or
biochemistry laboratories in a few days without requiring repeated purification.
Alternatively, institutional core facilities and commercial providers (e.g., GenScript,
Thermo Fisher Scientific, OriGene, Novus Biologicals) can supply purified protein at
modest cost. To support accessibility, we have deposited the Mj1640 expression plasmid
to Addgene.
Many widely used biochemical modification-mapping methods similarly make use of
purified enzymes (e.g., SAC-m6A-seq (PMID:35288668) and eTAM-seq for m6A (PMID
36593412)).
Advantages of ELAP-seq: 1) a high signal-to-noise ratio; 2) low sequencing depth and
computational demand compared to non-enrichment-based methods, making it cost- and
time-efficient; and 3) requiring a lower RNA input compared to earlier enrichment-based
Ψ mapping strategies.
Broad value of this study to the Ψ community: In addition to developing ELAP-seq, this
study establishes an efficient and specific enzymatic labeling assay for pseudouridine.
The labeling reaction, combined with click chemistry, offers a versatile platform for
potential future applications such as: 1) sensitive detection of Ψ for diagnosis purposes
(based on new data in Figure S4 and page 7, lines 142-157); 2) enrichment of modified
RNAs for interactome studies; and 3) compatibility with future low-input or in-cell
adaptations.
Major comments:
1. The authors claim that ELAP-seq could be used in live cells for Ψ profiling, but in the
ELAP-Seq protocol they denature fragmented isolated RNA prior to enzymatic labeling.
This is a contradiction, because RNA secondary structure is influenced by conditions
unique to cells not present in denatured fragmented isolated RNA, including long-range
RNA-RNA interactions and RNA-binding proteins. For this reason, it is not obvious to the
reader that in situ ELAP-Seq would work. Certainly in vivo ELAP-Seq, as hinted at in
Supplementary Fig. S3, would not work.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the
current ELAP-seq protocol involves denaturation of fragmented, isolated RNA prior to
enzymatic labeling, and that such conditions differ from those in live cells. In our study,
we observed that when the enzyme is expressed in mammalian cells, it can label
endogenous modifications with approximately 10% efficiency. The apparently lower
labeling efficiency in cells compared to that in vitro (Figure 1) may be due to factors
affecting accessibility of the enzyme to RNA such as protein protection, RNA tertiary
structure, and local enzyme versus substrate concentrations.
We agree that the current protocol is not yet optimized for in situ or in vivo mapping,
and
we have now toned this down in the main text to avoid overclaiming. Future
optimizations may enable these applications, such as fusing it with helicase or strand-
displacement domains, to transiently unwind structured RNAs for better labeling.
Despite this, our data show that the enzyme is catalytically active in cells and thus has
potential for in-cell labeling of pseudouridine. We envision that this system could be
developed further as an in-cell site-directed RNA modification tool, where a guide RNA
will be used to disrupt local RNA structure, similar to other RNA-guided modification or
editing systems. Since pseudouridine modification is irreversible, no current method
exists to specifically remove it at defined sites to study its biological function. We
propose that our approach could be used to perturb this modification and investigate its
functional role. We highlight this as a potential future application in the discussion
section (page 29, lines 586-591).
2. In the Introduction, the authors emphasize that many other methods for profiling Ψ
sites require a high level of RNA input and/or deep sequencing. Although the authors
showed the detection sensitivity of this assay on synthesized oligos in Figure 2b, the
detection limit of this assay on real mRNA samples from cells is unclear (based on the
Methods section, ELAP-seq appears to be carried out with 200-1000ng of RNA, but it is
unclear if it is total RNA or isolated mRNA). In this aspect, it remains uncertain whether
ELAP-seq can be used for rare cell populations that other methods could hardly
approach.
Our response: In the Introduction, we referred specifically to CeU-seq, which functions
similarly to ELAP-seq as an enrichment-based Ψ mapping method, that requires much
higher RNA input (10 µg of mRNA, approximately 50-fold higher) than our method.
Similarly, another enrichment-based method using antibody also requires 10 µg of
mRNA (Campos et al., PMID: 34376564). For other existing methods, our discussion
focused primarily on their need for deep sequencing, rather than their RNA input
requirements. We have further clarified this in the Discussion, under the section of
Advantages and Limitations of ELAP-seq (page 27, line 532).
As stated in the materials and method section, 200–1000 ng of RNA (mRNA) was used
for the initial fragmentation step, with a typical yield of ~80-100%. From this fragmented
RNA, we aliquoted ~200 ng for downstream library preparation. Therefore, ELAP-seq
currently requires ~250 ng mRNA input and is comparable to PRAISE in input
requirements (500 ng mRNA). These details were included in the original version and are
now further clarified in the revised Materials and Methods section (page 34, lines 692-
693).
Enrichment-based methods generally require higher RNA input than non-enrichment-
based approaches, due to loss of materials during binding and washing. ELAP-seq uses
mild labeling conditions, which preserves RNA, and the streptavidin-biotin pair, which
provides high binding affinity and can withstand stringent washes. These features make
the required RNA input lower than previous enrichment-based methods and comparable
to that of recent non-enrichment-based methods.
We clarify that the current implementation is not intended for rare-cell applications. It is
noteworthy that the use of a low dNTP concentration in our library preparation pipeline
necessitates a starting material of 250 ng of mRNA. We are actively developing a next-
generation, low-input version that does not require low dNTP or enrichment, enabling
substantially lower input requirements and reduced background.
3. In lines 234-236 the authors decided to use data generated with Superscript III for
detecting Ψ sites, while in lines 287-289 the authors decided to combine Superscript III
and Superscript IV data to yield better signal. The inconsistency of data analysis makes it
difficult to follow. It might be better to fix a filtering and cutoff strategy with rRNA
benchmarking and then stick to the same filtering so that the level of false positives can
be more easily estimated.
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comments about the inconsistency in data
analysis. We have now explained the rationale for using Superscript III and IV data. We
also applied refined and fixed filtering criteria throughout the analysis. These criteria
were first benchmarked using rRNA to ensure robustness before being applied to mRNA
data. This new analysis changed the numbers of identified candidate modification sites to
5,366 and 5,741 for HeLa and HEK293T poly(A) RNAs, respectively. We have updated
the manuscript throughout accordingly.
We have modified the main text to clarify the usage of Superscript III and IV (page 15-
16, lines 291-306):
“While Superscript III with low dNTP produces prominent RT stop signature, we noticed
that the coverage at some sites in mRNA is below the reads coverage cutoff although
both replicates share strong stop pattern. To achieve higher read coverage, we also used
superscript IV with the commercially recommended concentration of dNTP (0.5 mM
final) to generate libraries in parallel from the same pull-down product. Interestingly,
superscript IV also generated stop signatures at Ψ, although to a lesser extent (Figure
S7a), suggesting that the on-bead RT reaction used in our library construction protocol
further facilitated the generation of the stop signature (Figure S7a). To rescue additional
sites by increasing the reads coverage, we combined data from superscript IV and III for
further analysis. We first tested this analysis strategy on rRNA and verified that, with
slightly more stringent cutoff in stop ratio (See Materials and Methods section), this
strategy did not introduce additional false positives. Additionally, this analysis enabled
the identification of the two modification sites in 5.8S rRNA, which were previously
missed due to low coverage (Figure S7e).
Applying the same analysis on mRNA identified an additional 1,628 and 2,410 candidate
sites from HeLa and HEK293T poly(A) RNA, respectively, yielding a total of 5,366
candidate sites for HeLa and 5,741 for HEK (Figure 4d, Figure S9b). Of these, 2, 531
candidate Ψ sites are shared between HEK293T cells and HeLa cells, accounting for
~46% of all candidate sites in each cell line (Figure 4f). We note that some sites passing
the filter in one cell line but found in only one replicate in the other cell line were not
included. Therefore, the actual number of shared sites between the two cell lines may be
higher than reported here.”
We have updated and moved the description of the filter criteria to the Materials and
methods section:
On page 39-40, lines 813-823: “A candidate site in rRNA is defined when meeting the
following criteria: 1) the stop ratio at the site in the pull-down library is > 0.05 in both
replicates; 2) stop ratio in the pull-down library – stop ratio in the input library is > 0.05
in both replicates; 3) the number of stopped reads in the pull-down library is >=5 in both
replicates; 4) the average value of stop ratio * stopped reads between the two pull-down
replicates is >=1.5 (this imposes a more stringent requirement on the number of stopped
reads when the stop ratio in the pull-down sample is lower than 30%); and 5) the stop
event occurs at uridine (U). Finally, we further remove sites meeting the following
criteria: 1) the stop ratio in the input library is > 0.1 and > 1/3 of the stop ratio in the pull-
down library, and 2) number of stopped reads in input is > =3 in any replicate. When
using superscript III and IV data together, we follow the same criteria except for
requiring that the stop ratio in the pull-down library- stop ratio in the input library is >
0.1.”
We have added more details about the library preparation:
On page 36, lines 730-733: “Beads after pull-down were divided to two parts for the
downstream reverse transcription step, with three-quarters (corresponding to 150 ng
starting RNA) used for SuperScript III RT and one-quarter (corresponding to 50 ng
starting RNA) for SuperScript IV RT.”
4. In lines 278-280 and a few cases later in the manuscript, as well as in Fig. 4c-e, the
authors detected Ψ sites at U, G, A, C with different proportions, while when describing
their filter strategy (lines 246-247) they only include sites for which “the stop event
occurs at uridine (U).” It is unclear why these G, A, C sites were still included with their
pipeline, unless the authors really mean ΨU, ΨG, ΨA, and ΨC.
Our response: We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point. The figures in Fig. 4c–e
show the distribution of reverse transcription (RT) arrest sites at A, U, C, and G, rather
than the final calls of pseudouridylation. Only U positions exhibiting RT-stop signatures
are subsequently defined as candidate Ψ sites. Our analysis pipeline records RT stops at
all four nucleotides (A, U, C, G), but eventually filters for stop events occurring at U to
identify potential Ψ modification sites. To be clear, we do not infer pseudouridylation at
G, A, or C; these positions are presented solely to illustrate background RT-arrest
frequencies and to assess specificity, as elaborated below.
For mRNA, where modification sites are largely unknown, evaluating stops across non-U
nucleotides provides a measure of specificity and potential false positives. This is based
on the rationale that, if no specific labeling and enrichment of pseudouridine occurs, RT
stop would occur randomly with similar frequencies at A, U, C and G. Instead, we
observed strong U-specific enrichment (>95% for SuperScript III and >90% for
SuperScript IV) of RT stop signatures in the pull-down samples whereas input samples
showed no such enrichment, confirming that detected stops are specific to pseudouridine,
rather than resulting from RNA structure or sequencing artifacts. Similar specificity
analyses have been used in prior studies (Zhang et al.,PMID 26075521 and Cui et al.,
PMID 33313824).
In contrast, for rRNA, we omitted reporting results at non-U because the well-
characterized Ψ modification sites on rRNA can be directly used for specificity
validation, and we don’t need to use the data at non-U sites for this analysis. For rRNA,
only two non-U stops were detected (Supplementary table 5), consistent with the very
low false positive rate and supporting the reliability of using non-U stops to assess
specificity in mRNA.
In summary, non-U positions are included in the pipeline for specificity assessment in
mRNA. Only the U sites are further defined as Ψ modification sites. We have now further
clarified this in the main text (page 15, lines 277-290).
5. In the paragraphs to study Ψ sites in response to IFN treatment, the phenotype was not
well explained. By LS-MS/MS, there seemed to be a 20-25% reduction of global Ψ, while
by ELAP-seq there seemed to be 41-52% fewer sites. The authors should explain this
discrepancy. Additionally, since the protein level of PUS enzymes did not change, it is
unclear how robust this assay was. The authors should either demonstrate Ψ change with
a different method or identify other enzymes/regulators to explain the phenotype.
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the
discrepancy between LC-MS/MS and ELAP-seq results. The discrepancy likely arises
from the different nature of the two assays: LC-MS/MS quantifies the total Ψ content at
the nucleotide level, whereas ELAP-seq detects site-specific Ψ modifications, which
depend on detection thresholds. As shown in the figure below, the sites that become
undetectable after IFN treatment exhibit substantially lower read coverage than sites that
remain detectable. Thus, a modest reduction in modification level could cause many low-
coverage sites to fall below the ELAP-seq detection threshold, resulting in a larger
apparent decrease in the number of detectable sites (~41–52%) than in total Ψ abundance
(~20–25%).
We agree with the reviewer that the study of the IFN treatment is incomplete due to the
unresolved mechanism underlying Ψ downregulation phenotype. Fully resolving the
mechanism would require further investigation beyond PUS protein abundance,
potentially involving post-translational regulation, protein subcellular localization,
substrate availability, or unknown RNA-binding regulators. As this mechanistic
clarification is beyond the scope of the present study, we have removed the IFN treatment
data from this manuscript (previously Figure 6 and S17) and updated the text
accordingly. We are actively continuing this line of research as part of a follow-up study.
Importantly, this removal does not affect the robustness of ELAP-seq for differential
modification analysis, which has been demonstrated in the DKC1 knockdown
experiment. In the DKC1 knockdown experiment, the DKC1-dependent sites determined
by PRAISE are also predominantly downregulated in our dataset, supporting the reliable
detection of site-specific differential modification using our method.
In addition, this removal does not affect the core findings of the paper, which center on
(1) the biochemical characterization of Mj1640, (2) the development of ELAP-seq, and
(3) the validation of Ψ detection across transcriptomes.
In the revised version, we have strengthened the manuscript by adding new comparisons
with antibody-based detection methods (Figure S4, page 7 lines 142-157) and control
spike-in validation data (Figure S5), refining the ELAP-seq analysis pipeline, and
expanding discussion of future applications.
6. Pull-down of both enzymatic and control reactions in ELAP-seq means that the
methodology will likely be even less quantitative than other semi-quantitative methods for
lower RNA inputs. It is hard to imagine that spike-ins mentioned in lines 564-565 would
alleviate this concern.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this comment.
Pull-down of the control group is used solely as quality control during library
preparation. Under the same conditions, only modified RNAs in the experimental group
are expected to be successfully pulled down and yield detectable libraries, whereas the
control group is expected to produce no DNA in the end (Figure S9a), unless being
overamplified relative to the experimental group. Therefore, the control reaction does not
proceed to sequencing and is not required for data analysis.
In our analysis pipeline, quantification starts with calculating the enrichment level at each
site, defined by normalizing the RPM at that site in the pull-down sample by that in the
input sample to account for gene expression difference. This enrichment value is further
normalized to account for sequence context difference, generating the normalized
enrichment. The relative values of normalized enrichment reflect the relative
modification levels across different sites. Importantly, our measurements showed
moderate to high correlations with other quantitative methods at overlapping sites (Figure
4j and S15e). Based on these correlations, we determined the correlation between the
values of normalized enrichment and absolute modification levels, and then accordingly
assigned remaining non-overlapping sites to various modification level categories (Figure
S15f and the Materials and Methods section).
We envision that including barcoded spike-ins in various sequence contexts with defined
modification stoichiometries can improve the current quantification strategy. These
spike-ins will undergo the same enzymatic labeling and pull-down treatments as
biological RNAs, providing calibration curves that allow direct estimation of
modification levels in various sequence contexts. Such spike-in calibration methods have
been adopted by many studies (e.g., BACS (PMID:39349603) and PRAISE
(PMID:36997645)).
We also note that reads coverage can influence quantification accuracy: mRNA sites in
the ΨU context, rRNA sites and mRNA sites in the non-ΨU context readily detectable by
CLAP, which generally have high read coverage, correlate better with PRAISE
quantification than mRNA sites in non-ΨU context, which generally have low read
coverage (Figure 4i and S15e). Therefore, optimizing enzyme sequence preference will
also help to address concerns about quantification accuracy. We have now updated the
discussion section to further clarify this (page 27, lines 536-544).
Minor comments:
1. In the rebuttal, the authors write that, “Performed knockdown experiment for one of
the pseudouridine writers, DKC1, which led to the identification of 1014 sites confidently
downregulated due to DKC1 depletion, including 882 sites newly identified by ELAP-seq
(Figure 4h and the new supplementary Figure S10).” The authors should analyze how
much of this change is due to transcript expression changes leading to lower confidence
in calling Ψ sites vs. bona fide Ψ downregulation.
Our response: Our method to measure differential RNA modification uses changes in the
enrichment level, defined as the RPM in the pull-down library normalized by that in the
input library (please see main text at page 20, lines 380-381 and Material and Method
section at page 42, lines 874-876), which already takes into account the change in the
transcriptional expression level. Therefore, these are bona fide downregulation, instead of
false positives due to a decrease in the gene expression.
2. In line 114, the authors write, “data not shown.” They should show the data or
remove/restate the sentence.
Our response: Thank the reviewer for pointing this out. Since these negative data were
not systematically documented for inclusion in the manuscript, we have now removed
this sentence.
3. In line 232-234, the authors do not show Superscript IV data.
Our response: This data has now been shown in figure S7a.
4. The authors should state the precise statistical test used to generate the p-value stated
in line 241.
Our response: Please see the updated filtering and cutoff strategy in the Materials and
Method section (page 39-40, lines 813-823).
5. In line 466, Fig. 5f should be Fig. 5e.
Our response: This has been fixed.
6. In the Discussion in lines 604-605, the authors speculate that Mj1640 could be used to
selectively introduce m1Ψ to mRNA vaccines. It is hard to imagine that such a strategy
would be productive, given that such a change would inherently increase immunogenicity
and reduce protein translational efficiency.
Our response: We originally proposed such an application based on the hypothesis that
the modification may work through decorating a structurally important region in RNA
(Nance and Meier, PMID 34075344). However, a recent publication revealed that the
modification inhibits TLR7 and TLR8 activation through blocking degradation by
RNAse T2 (Bérouti et al., PMID 40580950), making our original hypothesis less likely.
Therefore, we have deleted this from the discussion. We have added other potential
applications for our method in the discussion section (page 29-30, lines 583-598).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Regarding the first point, while the inclusion of the spike-in results in Figure S5 is appreciated,
the color scheme requires adjustment as it is currently visually harsh. Additionally, the figure
legend needs to be expanded to provide more detailed descriptive information.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. Figure S5 has now been
updated with a different color scale, and the legend has been expanded with more details.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks on code availability):
The provided code is user-friendly and the documentation is sufficient. I was able to replicate
the installation and execution processes seamlessly.
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In their updated manuscript, Wang et al. substantially improve their report on the
enzymebased pseudouridine detection method ELAP-Seq. Beyond demonstrating enhanced
sensitivity of the method, they have removed incomplete data and unsupported claims. With a
few minor changes, their work could be suitablel for publication in Nature Communications.
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments of our revised manuscript.
1. The authors should add accessibility information on the Addgene-deposited Mj1640
expression plasmid to the Materials and Methods.
Our response: We have added the deposit ID of the plasmid in the Materials and Methods
paper (page 30). The plasmid will be released after the publication of this manuscript.
2. The authors should remove references to the interferon treatment experiment from the
Materials and Methods.
Our response: The section about interferon treatment has been removed from the Materials
and Methods section.
3. I am not convinced by the authors’ rebuttal to my previous minor comment 1.
a. For reference, I originally wrote: “In the rebuttal, the authors write that, “Performed
knockdown experiment for one of the pseudouridine writers, DKC1, which led to the
identification of 1014 sites confidently downregulated due to DKC1 depletion, including 882
sites newly identified by ELAP-seq (Figure 4h and the new supplementary Figure S10).” The
authors should analyze how much of this change is due to transcript expression changes
leading to lower confidence in calling Ψ sites vs. bona fide Ψ downregulation.”
b. The authors respond: “Our method to measure differential RNA modification uses
changes in the enrichment level, defined as the RPM in the pull-down library normalized by
that in the input library (please see main text at page 20, lines 380-381 and Material and
Method section at page 42, lines 874-876), which already takes into account the change in the
transcriptional expression level. Therefore, these are bona fide downregulation, instead of
false positives due to a decrease in the gene expression.”
c. The specific problem I have with this response is what the authors write in the previous
paragraph of their rebuttal: “We also note that reads coverage can influence quantification
accuracy: mRNA sites in the ΨU context, rRNA sites and mRNA sites in the non-ΨU context
readily detectable by CLAP, which generally have high read coverage, correlate better with
PRAISE quantification than mRNA sites in non-ΨU context, which generally have low read
coverage (Figure 4i and S15e).”
d. There appears to be a clear contradiction—if lower read coverage results in lower
quantification accuracy, presumably it also results in lower confidence of called Ψ sites. If this
is true, then decreased gene expression can indeed lead to an increase in sites confidently
downregulated. As is common in RNA enrichment method benchmarking, the authors should
perform additional analysis of their RNA-seq data (Fig. S12a). Specifically, they should assess
the degree to which genes harboring 717 (previously 1014—I am not sure what caused the
change) Ψ sites confidently downregulated are themselves downregulated in gene expression.

all RNA-Seq genes with the genes harboring these 717 Ψ sites plotted in a different color.
Additionally, they should quantify the distribution in fold-change of the Ψ site-harboring
genes relative to the fold-change of all genes. Such analysis will suitably resolve this open
question.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and apologize for not
previously fully addressing the concern. We now understand that the key issue is whether
reduced gene expression upon DKC1 knockdown could lead to insufficient starting material
for efficient pull-down and thereby cause apparent downregulation rather than true
modification level change. Our analyses below indicate that the degree of gene expression
change is insufficient to affect the confident detection of downregulated Ψ site, which are
now incorporated into Figure S12d–g.
When evaluating modification level changes, we used enrichment level at the modification
site, which is defined as the local read coverage per million mapped reads (RPM) in the pull-
down library normalized by that in the input library, which accounts for changes in
expression levels (a strategy similarly applied in analyzing differential modification in
MeRIP-seq data). To evaluate how much of this observed change is due to transcript
expression changes leading to lower confidence in calling Ψ sites versus bona fide Ψ
downregulation, we performed the analysis described below:
1. We analyzed differential gene expressions for genes harboring the downregulated
modification sites and for all genes detected by RNA-seq using data from the input
libraries (prior to pull-down), using DESeq2. We first looked at overall trends of gene
expression changes without applying cutoffs for p-value or fold change, and the
results are presented in figure S12d-f. The results showed that there is an equal
distribution of upregulation and downregulation for all genes (Figure S12d-e),
whereas there are more genes being downregulated than being upregulated for
genes harboring the downregulated modification sites (Figure S12d-e). The median
values of gene expression fold-changes are 1.03 for all genes and 0.83 for genes
harboring the downregulated modification sites (Figure S12f). When applying a p-
value cutoff of 0.05, only 262 genes harboring the downregulated modifications are
confidently downregulated, and when additionally applying a fold-change cutoff of
2, only 2 genes cross the thresholds (Figure S12d). These overall suggest that
although the expression of genes harboring the downregulated modification sites
tend to be overall downregulated upon DKC1 knockdown, the extent of that
downregulation is mild. Given that modification level changes were assessed by
normalizing pull-down-RPM values by input-RPM values to account for gene
expression changes, and that stringent cutoffs (p-value < 0.05 and fold change > 2)
were applied to define downregulated sites, the mild gene expression changes are
unlikely to affect the accuracy of the differential modification analysis.
2. To further evaluate whether the reduced gene expression after DKC1 knockdown
could prevent efficient pull-down in the absence of true modification changes, we
performed an additional analysis. Genes harboring Ψ sites detected before
knockdown represent transcripts with sufficient expression levels to support reliable
pull-down and modification detection. Under the assumption that Ψ modification
levels remain unchanged, transcripts whose post-knockdown expression levels
remain within this range should still be efficiently pulled down. To test this, we
compared the distribution of normalized gene-level read counts for genes harboring
downregulated Ψ sites after DKC1 knockdown with the distribution for all genes
harboring Ψ sites prior to knockdown. We found that these distributions are highly
comparable (Fig S12g), suggesting that despite modest expression decreases, the
post-knockdown expression levels remain sufficient for efficient pull-down (Fig 12g).
Based on these results, we updated the main text on page 17: “The changes in
expression of genes harboring these downregulated sites are mild and unlikely to
substantially affect the efficiency of pull down of this modification or the reliability of
the detected Ψ downregulation events (Figure S12d-g).”
3. To further increase the confidence in calling downregulated Ψ sites, we applied
additional conservative filtering in this revision. Specifically, from the list of
downregulated sites, we removed sites with average pull-down RPM values < 1.2
before treatment (corresponding to at least 10× local read coverage at the
modification given the current sequencing depth of (6-10M mapped reads)), as such
low-coverage sites are more susceptible to technical variation or subtle decrease in
gene expression. This filtering reduced the number of confidently downregulated Ψ
sites to 654. The updated results are shown in Fig. 4h.
Additionally, to focus on genes with considerable expression levels and to enable
more reliable quantification of enrichment fold change, readers can apply a cutoff of
1 for Input-RPM under both siCtrl and siDKC1 conditions (which corresponds to at
least 10x local read coverage at the modification under the current sequencing depth
(10-20 M mapped reads) (PMID: 31870409)). Notably, 81% of the downregulated
sites are above this cutoff, suggesting high reliability for most sites. This cutoff can
be user-defined based on their sequencing depth and research needs.
These changes have been incorporated into the Materials and Methods section: “For
downregulated sites, we further excluded sites with average pull-down RPM values <
1.2 before treatment (corresponding to approximately 10× local read coverage given
the current total mapped reads of 6-10M), as their enrichment measurements are more
susceptible to technical variation. For more reliable fold-change quantification,
readers can apply a cutoff of 1 for Input-RPM under both siCtrl and siDKC1 conditions,
which corresponds to at least 10x local read coverage given the current total mapped reads of
10-20 M. Such cutoff can be user-defined based on their sequencing depth and
research needs” (page 44)
4. For clarity, the reduction in the number of downregulated Ψ sites across manuscript
revisions reflects the cumulative application of increasingly stringent analysis criteria,
rather than changes in the underlying biological conclusions. During the last revision,
we applied an improved and more stringent analysis pipeline which has decreased
the total number of confident modification sites detected before treatment and
consequently reduced the number of sites identified as downregulated upon DKC1
knockdown. The additional conservative filtering applied in the current revision
further refined this list.
