Furthermore, our data covered 70% of TruB1 sites reported by PRAISE (Figure S10h) and all
mitochondria mRNA sites reported by PRAISE and BID-seq (Supplementary table 3-4).
Notably, by comparing the U sites and non-U sites identified by our method, we found that
increasing cutoff for stop ratio could increase the degree of confidence for the reported sites
(Figure 4 g-h). Additionally, by performing a third replicate for each cell line, we found that the
degree of confidence increases with the number of replicates (Figure 4i). This suggests a means
to better characterize the authenticity of each candidate site. Based on these observations, we
more stringently defined the degree of confidence for each candidate Ψ site based on the stop
ratio and the number of replicates the site can be repetitively identified in. Among the 10106
sites identified from HeLa cells, 4260 are defined as “highest-confidence” sites as they fulfil
both criteria of being identified in all three biological replicates and having stop ratios higher
than 0.3, 3801 sites are defined as “higher-confidence” sites for fulfilling one of the criteria, and
2044 are defined as “lower-confidence sites” for fulfilling none of the criteria (Figure 4j and
Lines 329-336).
The assignment of confidence, coupled with the enhanced accuracy in estimating the
modification levels as addressed in the response to question #2 from reviewer #1, provides
valuable insights for characterizing each individual candidate site.
Upon inspecting raw signals in BID-seq for 6,333 ELAP-seq-only higher or highest-confidence
sites, we found that 3,012 sites showed deletion ratio of higher than 0.05 in at least one replicate
of BID-seq, thus these sites demonstrate modification signals in BID-seq as well (Figure S10j).
Among the rest sites, 2,139 sites have deletion ratio of between 0.0 and 0.05 in BID-seq with
82% of them having average deletion ratios among three replicates of between 0.02 to 0.05,
which is below the deletion ratio cutoff used by the method (Figure S10j). There are 1,182 sites
having deletion ratio of 0 in BID-seq data, and these sites exhibited substantially lower read
coverage than sites detected by BID-seq, suggesting that these sites were missed by BID-seq due
to low gene expression (Figure S10k). This further supports the authenticity of sites identified by
ELAP-seq and underscores the high sensitivity of our approach in validating weak signals in
BID-seq.
In addition to more thorough data analysis, we also performed CLAP and CMC-RT-qPCR
validation for more sites. In addition to the ten sites presented in the previous version, we
evaluated 1 more site using CLAP (Figure S9c) and 7 more sites using CMC-RT-qPCR (Figure
S7f). Overall, 18 sites were successfully validated, including 10 sites not previously identified by
any method.
We have incorporated the above results in the revised manuscript (Lines 398-433), as well as
detailed discussions for the origins of false positives and false negatives to address concerns
users might have when approaching our dataset or using our method (Lines 573-607).
In response to reviewer’s suggestions, we employed siRNA knockdown (KD) of TruB1 and
DKC1 and strived to assess the dependence of our reported sites on PUS to further prove their
authenticity. Unfortunately, we have encountered unforeseen technical issues which have
delayed our data acquisition. We believe that the significant improvements we have made would
have already sufficiently addressed the concerns raised by the reviewers. Therefore, we are
submitting this revised manuscript without the inclusion of data from the PUS KD studies.
However, we are still actively acquiring data from the PUS KD experiments and will be willing
to provide the data if the reviewers see them remain necessary and critical.
We believe that this revised manuscript has been substantially improved by: 1) a more rigorous
characterization of the confidence level for each candidate site; 2) a comprehensive comparison
of our dataset with PRAISE and BID-seq to address the discrepancies; 3) improved accuracy in
quantifying the modification levels; 4) thorough evaluation of the reproducibility of our method;
5) site-specific validation of more sites not captured by other methods; 6) detailed discussions of
the origins of false negatives and false positives; as well as 7) streamlined pipeline with a single
command for user-friendly analysis. We believe these revisions have greatly increased the
usability of our dataset and the reliability of our method.
In summary, our revision includes additional experiments, meticulous data analysis, and detailed
discussions, reinforcing the validity of the identified sites. Moreover, our method excels in
detecting sites overlooked by other methodologies albeit may be less effective in identifying sites
in less favorable sequence contexts, especially those with low modification levels. We posit that
our method represents a potent innovation and serves as a crucial complement to the existing
toolbox for RNA modification detection and investigation.
2. The authors claim that 1/3 of sites have over a 50% modification rate, much higher than the
average mRNA modification rates estimated from other methods such as BID-Seq, and
inconsistent with their claim that the massive number of new sites are from enrichment of lowly-
modified positions. The authors must more rigorously demonstrate that their estimation of
modification occupancy is accurate, by correlating their estimates with estimates from
mutational-profiling methods such as BID-Seq, and by demonstrating correlation with many
more than 2 sites estimated by CLAP. Also, the CLAP vs ELAP-Seq comparison is difficult to
see in figure 4h and should have its own figure panel (with the additional comparisons).
Our response:
Thank the reviewer for this constructive critique. In response to the reviewer's critique, we
conducted a correlation analysis comparing the quantification results obtained from ELAP-seq
with those from CLAP and PRAISE (Lines 379-397). We performed CLAP and obtained
absolute quantification for one mRNA modification site (Figure S9c). In addition, there are 9
other mRNA modification sites quantified by CALP previously. All these 10 mRNA sites are in
non-ΨU sequence context. Notably, we observed a strong correlation between ELAP-seq and
CLAP quantifications for these sites (r = 0.83) (Figure 4m). Additionally, we correlated
quantification by our method to that by PRAISE due to a high number of overlapping sies. While
the correlations for sites within non-ΨU contexts were moderate (r = 0.46-0.56), the correlation
was high for sites within ΨU contexts (r = 0.72) (Figure S9d). These results, combined with the
observation that highly modified rRNA sites are distributed at the upper end of the quantification
spectrum, underscore the general accuracy of quantification by ELAP-seq.
Our method relies on adjusted enrichment levels to estimate the relative modification levels,
rather than determining exact modification ratios, a limitation of pull-down based strategies.
Nevertheless, by utilizing the absolute quantification provided by CLAP (for non-ΨU context
sites) and PRAISE (for ΨU context sites) as benchmarks, we were able to estimate the
approximate modification levels more confidently in this revised manuscript. This analysis
revealed that approximately 20-25% of sites exhibit moderate modification levels (between 30%-
60%) or high modification levels (exceeding 60%), while over 70% of sites are characterized as
lowly modified (below 30%) (Figure S9e). These results align more closely with conclusions
drawn from other studies (PMID: 36997645 and 36302989). Such semi-quantitative estimations
of modification levels, coupled with the capacity to probe modification level changes across
conditions, would render our method applicable to a wide range of studies.
With the improved quantification accuracy, we re-examined enriched GO terms for genes
containing moderately and highly modified Ψ, and found a notable enrichment of categories
related to mitochondrial electron transport and ATP synthesis (Figure 5e) (Lines 459-470). This
finding aligns with the report that PUS1 is associated with mitochondrial myopathy and calls for
future investigation into the roles of Ψ in mitochondrial function and associated diseases.
3. The language explaining the rational for cutoffs and filtering is vague. Please provide specific
details with statistical justification for the following: “We optimized cutoffs for stop ratio and
reads coverage and allow for gradients of coverage for different ranges of stop ratios” [275-276]
“We required higher reads coverage for lower levels of stop ratios to decrease false positives”
[685-686] “We allowed slightly lower reads coverage for sites in the out-group” [688-689]
“…we screened cutoffs for stop ratios and coverage to find a balance between the number of
sites identified and percentage of U” [689-691]
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewers' feedback regarding the clarity of cutoffs and filtering rationale. The
cutoffs were determined empirically. Initially, we set a stop ratio of 0.1, guided by our visual
examination of IGV, which indicated that some clustered sites tended to exhibit low stop ratios.
Additionally, we allowed a read coverage of 5, a practice used in several other studies (PMID:
31548705 and 26075521). However, upon using the percentage of U as an indicator, we found
these cutoffs to be suboptimal (U% = 81%). Consequently, we further refined them with more
stringent cutoffs. The rationale behind this optimization was requiring higher read coverage for
sites with lower stop ratios. In addition, in-group sites situated inside of the enrichment peaks
typically had higher read coverage, thus necessitating overall higher coverage thresholds for
these sites. As the number of sites detected decreases with increasing U%, we settled on cutoffs
which gave U% of 87.9%. The script used has been provided in GitHub and the cutoffs can be
further user-defined for desired confidence. For example, users may raise the cutoffs for stop
ratio to filter for sites with higher confidence.
We have now provided the specific details in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 875-
880):“…The optimized process was as follows: 1) we required higher reads coverage for lower
levels of stop ratios to decrease rate of false positives: In-group: at least 6-read coverage for sites
with stop ratios > 0.8, at least 8-read coverage for sites with stop ratios ranging between 0.2 and
0.8 , and stopped reads of at least 11 for sites with stop ratios ranging between 0.1 and 0.2; Out-
group: at least 5-read coverage for sites with stop ratios > 0.8, at least 7-read coverage for sites
with stop ratios ranging between 0.2 and 0.8 , and stopped reads of at least 2 for sites with stop
ratios ranging between 0.1 and 0.2; …”
4. For the IFN dataset it is mentioned that “the interferon stimulated samples (IFN+) resulted in
~40% less reads compared to untreated samples (IFN-), thus we allowed lower reads coverage
cutoff for the IFN+ samples.”[715-719] How does this not increase the false positive rate for the
INF+ samples – if the read cutoffs were set to minimize false positive rate? Intuitively this cutoff
should not be determined by read depth. This comparison would be more accurate with the INF-
samples randomly sub-sampled down to the same depth as INF+, using identical read cutoffs.
Our response:
This is a great point. In the previous version of the manuscript, we implemented a stricter cutoff
for IFN- samples and a looser cutoff for IFN+ samples, based on the established thresholds used
for HeLa and HEK cell lines. As noted by the reviewer, this adjustment could lead to an
increased rate of false negatives and false positives for each sample group, respectively. In this
revised manuscript, we reverted to the original cutoffs, resulting in the identification of 9117 and
3737 candidate sites from IFN- and IFN+ samples, respectively (Figure 6c and Lines 498-501).
To ensure more accurate comparisons, we conducted a reanalysis of the data by employing an
equal number of sub-sampled reads for both IFN- and IFN+ samples. Utilizing the same pipeline
with consistent read cutoffs, we reanalyzed data subsampled from reads of libraries constructed
with SuperScript III, or combined libraries built with SuperScript III and SuperScript IV. In both
scenarios, we observed a 40~50% reduction in identified sites from the IFN+ samples compared
to the IFN- samples (Figure S12b and lines 501-503). This finding supports a consistent trend of
downregulation of Ψ following interferon treatment, which aligns with observations made using
LC-MS/MS.
Minor critiques:
1. “a significant proportion of Ψ sites in mRNA appear in the 5’-ΨU-3’ context…” [203-204]
what proportion exactly?
Our response: Based on the paper of Li et al., ~30% of Ψ sites appear in the 5’ ΨU 3’ context.
We have changed our main text to provide a more precise description (Lines 209-210).
2. “30 – 60% of Ψ in cellular mRNA can be labeled by this enzyme” [205-206] Do you expect
30-60% of Ψ positions are being labeled – or each site is being labeled at a 30-60% rate?
Our response:
We apologize for the confusion caused by this sentence. The ratio 30-60% is m1Ψ/Ψ percentage
determined through LC-MS/MS analysis on digested RNAs. Due to the sequence preference of
the enzyme, the efficiency of enzymatic labeling should be higher for Ψ sites in the 5’-ΨU-3’
context compared to sites in other sequence contexts. Ψ sites in the 5’-ΨU-3’ constitutes around
30% of all Ψ sites in mRNA while Ψ sites in other sequence contexts constitutes about 70%.
Therefore, more than 30% of Ψ sites would undergo labeling, with the degree of labeling at
individual positions contingent upon the specific sequence context, which together gave an
overall labeling efficiency of 30-60% across all Ψ sites.
We have modified our main text to clarify this (Line 139): “The overall 33-60% m1Ψ/Ψ ratio
suggests that a considerable proportion of Ψ modification sites were successfully labeled.”
3. Why is there a stop in untreated RNA at the expected psi position in figure 2e?
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewer's observation, and upon reflection, we acknowledge that our
manuscript lacked clarity in describing the experiment's design.
In our assay, we used a synthetic 33-mer RNA as the template, which harbors a Ψ modification
in the middle. A fluorescently labeled RT primer was designed to target the position immediately
downstream of the modification site. The RT primer and template were mixed at a 1:10 ratio to
drive most primers to hybridize with the template. In the absence of any treatment, the RT primer
reads through the modification site, producing the full-length RT product (upper FL band).
Conversely, when encountering the propargyl-Ψ adduct (with or without subsequent
biotinylation at a low dNTP concentration), the elongation of the RT primer is impeded, resulting
in a significant amount of un-extended RT primer (lower Primer band in Figure 2e).
The anticipated stop signatures in treated RNA align precisely with the expected Ψ position. The
limited presence of un-extended RT primer bands in untreated RNAs is likely attributed to a low
level of unhybridized RT primer (Figure 2e, lane 2 and lane 6). Notably, the un-extended RT
primer bands in treated RNAs exhibited considerably stronger signals compared to those in
untreated RNAs (Figure 2e, lane 3-5 compared to lane 2, and lanes 7-9 compared to lane 6). This
disparity indicates that the introduction of bulkier groups during Ψ labeling significantly
increased the arrest rate of reverse transcription at the modification site, aligning with our
expectations.
To make the experimental design clearer, we have incorporated additional details in the legend
of Figure 2 and in the Materials and Method section (Lines 714-724).
4. How do the NNpsiNN pools perform in the standard library prep? E.g. are there any RT-stop
or ligation biases due to sequence context?
Our response:
We appreciate the reviewer's insightful question. In assessing the sequence preference of
enzymatic labeling with the NNpsiNN pools, we employed a protocol designed to avoid
generating RT stops so that we could comprehensively evaluate the sequence context spectrum
on both sides of the modification site. Specifically, following on-bead pull-down, we eluted
RNAs from the beads by heat-denaturing the streptavidin-biotin interaction. Subsequently, we
employed Superscript IV with 0.5 mM final dNTP to facilitate full readthrough at the
modification site. Additional details about this methodology have been incorporated into the
Materials and Methods section for clarification (Lines 816-817).
Our ELAP-seq results consistently identified uracil as the primary nucleobase, aligning with the
in vitro characterization of Mj1640's specificity towards Ψ. This evidence supports the
conclusion that ELAP-seq specifically detects Ψ sites in RNA. We want to emphasize that, in our
library preparation workflow, we do not perceive sequence context-dependent biases in RT-stop
or ligation. While previous studies have reported sequence biases for 3’ RNA adapter ligation
using T4 RNA ligase 2 truncated KQ, we mitigated this bias by employing RNA adapters with
multiple Ns on the 5’ end, as recommended (Nucleic Acids Research, 2011, Nov; 39(21):e141).
Our analysis of input libraries using the same pipeline revealed no enrichment for uracil,
demonstrating that ligation and reverse transcription were not influenced by sequence context.
5. It is not described how the wobble pair analysis was performed, please add more detail in the
methods or main text.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have now provided a more detailed description
of the analysis in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 934-946). We have also deposited the
data analysis pipelines and the in-house python transcripts to GitHub.
“RNA sequences of 100 nt surrounding all Ψ sites located in different mRNA subregions (5’
UTR, 3’ UTR and CDS) with 50 nt upstream and 50 nt downstream were used for RNA
secondary structure prediction. The program viennaRNA was used with the command of
‘RNAfold -p < input.fa > output.res’. The resulting file was cleaned up in notepad++ to keep the
information of the topmost prediction for each site. Then, we used an in-house python script
match.py to extract the information of the base pairing status of the modification site and the
location of its matched base if it is base paired. We then determined the identity of the matched
base for each base-paired modification site using the ‘MID’ function in excel. Next, we
calculated the frequency of the modification site residing in a mismatched/UG wobble status
versus in UA matched status. Control U sites were chosen at both the -20 position and +20
position of Ψ sites and analysis were performed the same way as for Ψ sites. mfold were used to
draw the secondary structures of 100 nt surrounding the chosen Ψ sites.”
6. Enrichment of Ψ at splice junctions is only informative with a comparison against the
background distribution of U. Plot both distributions from your dataset and demonstrate that the
difference in Ψ distribution is significant.
Our response:
We express gratitude to the reviewer for providing valuable insights into the analysis. In
response to the suggestion, we randomly selected 10,000 U sites from the transcriptome and
conducted a parallel analysis. To our disappointment, these randomly chosen sites were also
found to be situated within 100 nt of the nearest splice sites. To delve deeper into this
observation, we computed the average distance to splice sites within 800 nt, 400 nt, 200 nt, and
100 nt windows, and still, no substantial differences were observed between the Ψ group and the
control U groups across any of these window sizes. We regret the oversight that led to an
incorrect conclusion in the previous version of the manuscript. To rectify this, we have removed
the erroneous figure and texts that depicted the correlation of Ψ with splicing.
